title: Why Podcasting Is the Ultimate Trust-Building Tool for Women Leaders
guestBio: Allison Hare is the creator of The Culture Changers, a top 1.5% globally ranked podcast with nearly one million downloads and guests including Seth Godin and Jesse Itzler. After 23 years in Fortune 500 corporate sales, she walked away to build a platform rooted in authentic voice and real influence. Today she coaches founders and leaders to launch podcasts that generate trust, visibility, and lasting authority.
excerpt: You're posting, showing up, and doing all the things — so why does it still feel like no one's really seeing you? Allison Hare, creator of the top 1.5% globally ranked Culture Changers podcast, joins Aimee to reveal why trust — not content volume — is the real currency of influence, and how podcasting is the vehicle that builds it faster than anything else.
metaDescription: Allison Hare reveals how podcasting builds trust, authority & real influence for women leaders — without chasing algorithms. Ep 71 of The Manage Her®.
keyTakeaways: Trust — not follower count or content volume — is the real currency of influence online, and podcasting is one of the most powerful vehicles for compounding it over time.
Your point of view is a lighthouse: a clear, specific perspective doesn't repel people — it attracts exactly the right ones and filters out everyone else.
You don't need credentials, a perfect setup, or a massive audience to deserve a microphone — you're already a few steps ahead of someone who is praying for exactly your help.
30 superfans who take action will always outperform 1,000 passive downloads, because influence is measured in transformation, not traffic.
Long-form content like podcasting lets potential clients, collaborators, and communities experience what it's actually like to be in your world before they ever reach out.
Visibility is not vanity — staying invisible is far more costly than the discomfort of being seen, misunderstood, or even disliked by the wrong people.
If the knock on the door of your purpose keeps getting louder, that is not a coincidence — it is your cue to answer it.

quiz.title: What Kind of Podcast Host Are You Meant to Be?
quiz.description: You know you have something to say. But how you're meant to say it — and why you've been holding back — is written all over your answers. Take this self-discovery quiz to uncover your podcasting archetype and what's really standing between you and your microphone.

A.name: The Authority Architect
A.description: You have deep expertise, a clear point of view, and a track record that speaks for itself — but you've been waiting for the "right moment" to put it all in one place. Your podcast isn't about building credibility from scratch; it's about making your existing authority undeniable and accessible. You have a tendency to over-prepare and under-publish, which means the people who need your voice most haven't found it yet. Episode 71 will give you the specific reframe you need to stop perfecting and start transmitting.

B.name: The Community Catalyst
B.description: You are magnetic in rooms — people lean in when you talk, remember what you said weeks later, and keep showing up wherever you are. Your podcast would not just build an audience; it would build a movement. You may have dismissed podcasting as too solo, too technical, or too much of a solo performance, but Allison's conversation with Aimee will reframe it as exactly the community-building tool you've been searching for. Your people are already out there — they just haven't heard your voice yet.

C.name: The Reluctant Visionary
C.description: You have a vision that is genuinely ahead of its time, and that has made you quietly terrified of being misunderstood. You've watched others speak on your ideas less eloquently and gotten more credit for it, and some part of you has decided that staying small is safer than being seen imperfectly. The "it is safe to be seen" moment in this episode was written for you — not as a motivational poster, but as a direct confrontation of the specific fear that's been keeping your voice locked away. Your reluctance is not modesty. It's protection. And it's costing you.

D.name: The Serial Storyteller
D.description: You have lived enough chapters to fill a bookshelf, and the through-line of your story has a clarity and weight that stops people mid-scroll. You may not think of yourself as an "expert" in any one thing, but you are a master of meaning-making — you know how to take experience and turn it into something someone else can use. Allison's dismantling of the expertise myth in this episode will land like a direct answer to the question you've been quietly asking for years: do I have enough to say? The answer, unequivocally, is yes.

content:
You are creating content. You are showing up. You are posting, repurposing, hashtagging, and doing the thing — and yet, something still feels hollow. You are everywhere, and somehow still invisible. If that sentence just landed somewhere in your chest, this episode was made for you.

In Episode 71 of The Manage Her® Podcast, Aimee Rickabus sits down with Allison Hare — creator of The Culture Changers, a top 1.5% globally ranked podcast with nearly one million downloads — for one of the most honest, energizing conversations this show has ever hosted. This is not a how-to on podcast gear. This is a conversation about what it actually costs you to stay hidden, and what becomes possible when you finally decide to be seen.

The Trust Recession Is Real — And Content Volume Won't Fix It

We are living through what Allison calls a trust recession. Audiences are more skeptical, more saturated, and more burned out on polished, performative content than at any point in history. The brands and voices that are winning right now are not the loudest — they are the most trusted. And trust, Allison argues, is not built through frequency. It is built through depth, consistency, and the courage to have a genuine point of view.

Podcasting, specifically, is the long-form medium that lets people experience what it is like to be in your world before they ever send you a DM, book a call, or buy your offer. It is an hour of unfiltered access to how you think, what you believe, and whether or not you are the real thing. That is not something a carousel post or a thirty-second reel can replicate. That is a relationship — and relationships are what convert.

Stop Sounding Like Everyone Else

One of the most important things Allison says in this conversation is that the biggest mistake new podcasters make is mimicking the hosts they admire. You listen to someone polished and authoritative, and your instinct is to sound like them — to adopt their cadence, their format, their energy. But the moment you do that, you disappear. The thing that makes a podcast magnetic is not production value. It is specificity of voice. Your weird, particular, unfiltered way of seeing things is not a liability. It is the whole point.

Allison also dismantles the expertise myth with surgical precision. You do not need a doctorate, a decade of experience, or a celebrity guest list to deserve a microphone. You are already ahead of someone who is just beginning. You have already lived through something someone else is still navigating in the dark. That gap — however small it feels to you — is exactly where your voice belongs.

"It Is Safe to Be Seen"

The most powerful moment of this episode comes at the 18-minute mark, when Allison shares the story of a stranger's notebook. Four words, written on a page she was never meant to see: It is safe to be seen. For high achievers — for women who have spent decades learning to be competent, capable, and contained — those words are not inspiration. They are confrontation. Because somewhere along the way, most of us learned that being visible also meant being a target. That standing out invited scrutiny. That having a strong opinion would cost us something.

Allison reframes this entirely. She points out that invisibility has its own cost — one we rarely audit honestly. The client who needed exactly what you offer but found someone else. The community that would have gathered around your voice but never knew you existed. The version of yourself that kept waiting for permission that was never coming. Being hated by the wrong people, she says, is infinitely better than being invisible to the right ones.

The Four Purposes of a Podcast — And Which One Is Yours

Around the 37-minute mark, Allison maps out the four real reasons to launch a podcast: credibility, networking, lead generation, and storytelling. This is where the conversation becomes genuinely practical. Not every podcast needs to be a top-of-funnel sales machine. For some women, the value is in the doors it opens — the guests you get to call peers, the stages that find you, the press that takes you seriously because you have a show. For others, it is about having a body of work that documents who you are and what you believe over time. Knowing your purpose before you hit record changes everything about how you show up.

Allison also introduces the honest trifecta of podcast readiness: budget, bandwidth, and burning desire. You do not need all three in abundance. But you do need to be honest about which one is actually the obstacle — and which one you are using as an excuse. The Blue Yeti microphone story that follows this is worth the entire episode on its own. Spoiler: the messy first episode is not the problem. It is, in fact, the whole point.

30 Superfans Will Change Your Life

In an era obsessed with download numbers and vanity metrics, Allison offers a radical recalibration. Thirty people who trust you, share your episodes, and act on what you say will do more for your business, your brand, and your sense of purpose than one thousand passive listeners ever will. Influence is not a volume game. It is a transformation game. And podcasting, done with intention and authenticity, is one of the few mediums left where that kind of transformation is still possible at scale.

If the knock on the door of this idea keeps getting louder every time you scroll past someone else's show — that is not a coincidence. That is your cue. This episode is your permission slip to answer it.
